cues.text: On Holy Thursday of 1417, in the town of Erding in Bavaria, a peasant stole a consecrated Host, apparently hoping the sacred object might bring him some material benefit or protection.
A Host That Would Not Be Carried
As he made his way from the church with the Host in hand, it escaped his grasp and rose into the air, hovering beyond his reach.
He grabbed for it repeatedly and, by some accounts, it slipped from him and rose again as many as three times before he was forced to give up the pursuit entirely.
Word of the strange event reached the local bishop, whose direct intervention finally ensured that the Host was recovered safely.
The surviving accounts do not detail its precise nature, resolving the extraordinary episode that had by then drawn considerable local attention.
A chapel was built without delay on the spot where the Host had finally come to rest.

In the years that followed, numerous cures and other favors were attributed to those who came to venerate it there—the kind of accumulating local testimony that, in this period, often turned a single strange event into a lasting regional shrine.
The Erding account belongs to a distinct pattern among medieval Eucharistic traditions in which the Host itself appears to resist improper handling.
It rises out of reach, refuses to be carried off, or otherwise eludes whoever would treat it as an ordinary object rather than a sacred one.
Whatever weight a modern reader gives to the specific details, the chapel raised on the spot testifies to how seriously the people of fifteenth-century Erding took what they believed had happened.
The devotion that gathered around it for generations afterward likewise reflects that seriousness in their own town square.
